title: Ramayana · Bala Kanda Part 1: From Valmiki's First Verse to Rama's First Battle
topic: Bala Kanda Part 1 (Valmiki Ramayana 1.1–1.30, cliff from 1.31): Narada's question, the krauncha birds and the first shloka, Brahma's charge; Ayodhya, the sacrifice and the four princes; Vishvamitra asks for Rama; Tataka and the divine weapons; the defence of the six-day sacrifice
edition: vulgate (southern recension), sa.wikisource; verse numbers cross-checked on valmikiramayan.net (Internet Archive copy) where noted

scenes.narration: His father said he was too young to fight rakshasas, and on the sixth day, they came.
scenes.tts: His father said he was too young to fight raakshasas, and on the sixth day, they came.

scenes.narration: Is there anyone in this world today, he asked, who is good and brave, who knows dharma, who is truthful and firm in his vows, who has conquered anger, and whom even the gods fear in battle?
scenes.visual: the verse written in chalk on the open dark board, wide horizontal layout

scenes.narration: Narada was glad at heart. Such qualities are rare, he said, yet one man has them all; he was born in the line of Ikshvaku, and the people call him Rama.
scenes.tts: Naarada was glad at heart. Such qualities are rare, he said, yet one man has them all; he was born in the line of Ikshvaaku, and the people call him Raama.

scenes.narration: Then he told Valmiki the whole of Rama's story and rose into the sky. Valmiki went down to the Tamasa river, and there, wandering the bank, he saw a pair of krauncha birds singing sweetly, never leaving one another's side.

scenes.narration: But before his eyes, a hunter with a heart full of malice shot down the male bird, and his mate, seeing him fallen on the earth, cried out in grief.

scenes.narration: Pity filled the sage's heart, and these words broke from him: hunter, may you never find rest through endless years, for you have struck down one of a pair lost in love.
scenes.visual: the verse written in chalk on the open dark board, wide horizontal layout

scenes.narration: Afterwards he wondered at his own words, for they had come out in four even lines, fit to be sung to the strings, and he said that this verse, born of sorrow, should be called a shloka.

scenes.narration: Later Brahma, the creator of the worlds, came to him and said: it was my will that this speech came to you, so tell all of Rama's story, and as long as mountains stand and rivers flow, it will be told. And so one sage's sorrow became a shloka, and the shloka became the Ramayana.

scenes.narration: The story he sang begins in Ayodhya, a city on the Sarayu built by Manu himself, and its king, Dasharatha, was truthful and wise and dear to all his people.

scenes.narration: Yet this great king had no son to carry on his line, and without one, he said, there was no joy for him.

scenes.narration: So he resolved on the great horse sacrifice; his priests, led by Vasishtha, blessed the plan, and the young sage Rishyashringa came to lead the rites on the bank of the Sarayu.

scenes.narration: When it was done, Rishyashringa lit one more fire for the birth of sons. The gods who gathered there for their share cried to Brahma in fear, for the rakshasa king Ravana, proud of his boon, was tormenting all three worlds, and even the sun dared not scorch him.

scenes.narration: He had asked to be safe from gods and demons, but in his scorn he never thought of men; and so the god Vishnu agreed to be born as a man, as the son of King Dasharatha.

scenes.narration: Then from the fire rose a radiant being, bright as the sun, holding a golden vessel of payasa made by the gods; give it to your queens, he said, and you will have sons.

scenes.narration: The king, like a poor man who has found treasure, gave half to Kausalya, half of what was left to Sumitra, half of the rest to Kaikeyi, and, after a moment's thought, the last share to Sumitra again.

scenes.narration: In the spring month of Chaitra, on the ninth day, Kausalya gave birth to Rama; Kaikeyi bore Bharata, and Sumitra bore Lakshmana and Shatrughna, and all Ayodhya filled with singing and dancing.

scenes.narration: The four princes grew in learning and in archery, and Lakshmana was like Rama's second life; Rama would not even sleep without him. And as the princes came of age, the king began to think of their weddings, never guessing who was about to come to his gate.

scenes.narration: I am keeping a sacred vow, the sage said, and two rakshasas, Maricha and Subahu, rain flesh and blood upon my altar; while the vow lasts I may not curse them, so give me Rama for ten nights.

scenes.narration: The king fell senseless, and when he came to himself he said: my lotus-eyed Rama is not yet sixteen, and I do not see him fit to fight rakshasas.

scenes.narration: Take my army instead, he begged, take me, for I cannot live a moment without Rama; and when he heard that Ravana stood behind these rakshasas, his fear only grew.

scenes.narration: At dawn the sage woke him gently: Kausalya is blessed in her son, Rama, the twilight is here, so rise, tiger among men; centuries later a temple hymn would open with these words. That morning they walked on toward the Ganga, and beyond it lay a dreadful forest, and the one who had laid it waste.

scenes.narration: Do not shrink from this because she is a woman, the sage told him; those who protect the people must act, cruel as the deed may seem, for that is the lasting duty of all who rule.

description: The first long-form chapter of RAMAYANA, The Epic in Chalk: how a sage's grief became the first shloka, how a childless king became the father of four princes, and how a boy not yet sixteen guarded a sacrifice for six sleepless days. Told from Valmiki's Ramayana, Bala Kanda sargas 1 to 31 (vulgate).

learnings.how: Partly applied. 'State the stakes early' is applied: the first line names the stake (a boy his father thought too young, and the rakshasas coming) and the cold open closes in about 27 s. The 35 s beat shape and the 18–25 s turn are Shorts-only and do not apply to the 8–12 min format.

Applied in its long-form form: a short, stakes-first first line (17 words, estimated 5.6 s, under the 6 s long-form warning; the 3.0 s Shorts limit does not apply). Frame 0 direction is the guarded fire under a roaring sky, readable muted.

Not applied in the narration: long-form has no engagement line and no subscribe lines. Suggested to the packager as a pinned comment with a real answer in the text: 'Which bird's death made the first shloka?' (the krauncha, 1.2.10–15).
